tasks.title: An lsns summary by type
tasks.statement: The input is the output of lsns with no arguments: columns NS TYPE NPROCS PID USER COMMAND, the first line is a header. The COMMAND field may contain spaces. Write a function lsns_report(text): return a list of tuples (type, number_of_rows, sum_of_NPROCS), one for every type that appears, sorted by type name. Skip blank lines and the header; empty output gives [].
tasks.hint: line.split(None, 5) keeps COMMAND whole; a data row starts with a number.

tasks.title: Namespaces two processes share
tasks.statement: You get two texts: the output of ls -l /proc/PID/ns for two processes. A link line looks like “lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 0 Nov  3 10:15 net -> 'net:[4026531840]'”; the quotes around the target may be present or absent. Skip lines without “ -> ” (for example “total 0”). The entry name is the last word before “ -> ”, the target is everything after “ -> ” without spaces and single quotes. Write a function shared_namespaces(a, b): return a sorted list of the names that appear in both texts and whose targets are equal (pid_for_children and time_for_children are separate names).
tasks.hint: Parse each text into a dictionary name -> target, then intersect the keys.

tasks.title: Translating an ID through uid_map
tasks.statement: A uid_map (or gid_map) file has lines of three numbers: “inside outside length”, separated by spaces of any width. A line describes the ranges [inside, inside+length) and [outside, outside+length), with the same offset in both. Write a function translate_id(map_text, ident, direction). For direction = "in2out" return the outside number for the number ident taken inside the namespace, or -1 if the map does not describe it inside. For direction = "out2in" return the inside number for the number ident taken outside, or 65534 if the map does not describe it outside (this is how a process sees an unmapped number by default).
tasks.hint: In every line check a <= ident < a + n (or b <= ident < b + n) and add the offset.

tasks.title: Is a uid_map write allowed
tasks.statement: We model a write to /proc/PID/uid_map or gid_map. Arguments: map_text is the text being written; writer is a dictionary {"privileged": bool, "euid": number, "kind": "uid" or "gid", "setgroups_deny": bool, "written": bool}; parent is a list of [start, length] pairs of the numbers that exist in the parent namespace. Write a function validate_map(map_text, writer, parent): return "ok", "EINVAL" or "EPERM". The checks, in order: 1) written is true: "EPERM" (the map is written once); 2) no lines at all, more than 340 lines, a line that is not three non-negative integers, a length below 1, overlapping ranges inside or overlapping ranges outside: "EINVAL"; 3) an outside range that does not fit entirely within one range of parent: "EPERM"; 4) if the writer is not privileged (no CAP_SETUID/CAP_SETGID in the parent): there must be exactly one line, of length 1, whose outside number equals the writer's euid, and for kind = "gid" setgroups_deny must be true; otherwise "EPERM". Otherwise "ok".
tasks.hint: First parse the lines into triples, then check in order; for overlaps sort the ranges by start.

tasks.title: Ids in ip netns list
tasks.statement: The output of ip netns list has one line per namespace: “name” or “name (id: N)” when the namespace has an identifier N. Write a function netns_ids(text): return a dictionary name → identifier for all namespaces. Give those without an identifier one the way “ip netns set name auto” does in our model: in line order, each gets the smallest non-negative number that is not yet taken (taken ones are those in the text and those already assigned). Skip blank lines and ignore spaces at the edges of a line.
tasks.hint: First collect the taken numbers from the whole text, then walk the lines without a number in order.

tasks.title: A container's namespaces from its options
tasks.statement: A Docker-like runtime gets the argument list of a run command. Write a function runtime_ns(args, userns_remap): return a dictionary with the keys "mnt", "pid", "net", "uts", "ipc", "user"; each value is "new" (the container has its own namespace), "host" (shared with the host) or "container:NAME" (shared with another container, the string exactly as in the argument). Rules. mnt is always "new". The options --pid, --uts, --ipc, --network (and its synonym --net) take the value either after = or as the next argument: "--pid=host" or "--pid", "host". The value "host" gives "host"; for pid, ipc and net a value starting with "container:" gives it whole; anything else (including a missing option, bridge, none, private, a user-defined network name) gives "new". For user: "--userns=host" (or "--userns", "host") gives "host"; without it the answer is "new" if the daemon runs with user remapping (userns_remap is true) and "host" otherwise. If an option is repeated, the last one wins. Ignore the other arguments (--name, -p, --hostname, --privileged, the image and their values).
tasks.hint: Walk the list by index: if the argument equals an option, the value is the next one; if it starts with “option=”, the value follows the sign.

tasks.title: unshare flags for a goal
tasks.statement: Choose the unshare flags. The function unshare_flags(want, proc, root, privileged): want is a list of the namespaces needed from "mnt", "uts", "ipc", "net", "pid", "cgroup", "time", "user"; proc says whether a fresh /proc is needed; root says whether you must be root inside (without being root outside); privileged says whether root runs the command. Return a sorted list of unique long flags. Mapping: mnt → --mount, uts → --uts, ipc → --ipc, net → --net, pid → --pid, cgroup → --cgroup, time → --time, user → --user. Rules: pid adds --fork; proc adds --mount-proc and removes --mount (it is implied); root replaces --user with --map-root-user (which implies a user namespace); an unprivileged run that needs any namespace other than user, or a fresh /proc, gets --user added (unless --map-root-user is on).
tasks.hint: Build a set of flags, apply the rules one by one, and end with sorted().

tasks.title: Host PID versus PID inside
tasks.statement: You get a list of texts: fragments of /proc/PID/status of different processes, as the host sees them. Each has an “NSpid:” line with the process numbers in all PID namespaces it belongs to: the first number is the number on the host, the last is the number in the innermost namespace; the numbers are separated by tabs or spaces. The other lines (Name:, Pid:, NStgid: and so on) are not needed; the NStgid, NSpgid and NSsid lines, which look similar, do not count. Write a function pid_pairs(statuses): return a list of tuples (host_number, inner_number), only for processes whose NSpid has at least two numbers (that is, which live in a nested namespace), sorted by the host number. Skip texts without an NSpid line.
tasks.hint: Look for a line that starts exactly with “NSpid:”, split the rest with split() and take the first and the last items.

tasks.title: A clock inside a time namespace
tasks.statement: The file /proc/PID/timens_offsets has lines “clock seconds nanoseconds”, where clock is monotonic or boottime; seconds may be negative, nanoseconds are non-negative. In our model, a clock reading inside the namespace equals the host's reading plus the offset (seconds·10^9 + nanoseconds). The realtime clock is not virtualized: inside, the reading is the same as on the host. If the file has no line for the clock, the offset is 0. Write a function timens_clock(offsets_text, clock, host_ns): clock is monotonic, boottime or realtime, host_ns is the host's reading in nanoseconds; return the reading inside the namespace in nanoseconds, or -1 if the result would be negative.
tasks.hint: Parse lines into a dictionary clock -> (sec, ns), then host_ns + sec*10**9 + ns.
